### Add Box Office, a distributed ticketing system to verify

[`74d96ec54e53`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/74d96ec54e5327fdc089afd91f4c2e647c2d8e3a) · [log `5ec7a7c2be3b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/560d5e98-2825-4bc2-90e2-39953d65d9c0/5ec7a7c2be3bc8d7d07ccbc6181db008eb1084fb143b025e4fa0da82c7553737.jsonl.gz)

apps/boxoffice is a Gradle multi-module build (Java 25, Spring Boot 4.1.1) with two services, ticketing and payments, that share nothing but Kafka topics. Ticketing exposes synchronous capabilities (create a concert, see availability, hold seats under a lease with all-or-nothing semantics) and asynchronous ones (place and cancel orders, answered 202 and settled by a saga with the payment service). Each service owns a MongoDB database and uses a transactional outbox, an idempotent inbox, conditional updates, transaction retry and dead-letter topics. A late payment for an expired hold, and a cancellation, are compensated by a refund.

The order state machine and seat rules are pure Java in ticketing-domain, as the first target for verification tools. The README states the safety and liveness invariants the verification scenarios should establish, and lists known gaps (relay without a lease, clock skew, gateway call inside a transaction) as scenarios for tools to find.

Verified with ./gradlew build: 29 tests pass. They include a bounded model check of every order input sequence up to six inputs, a component test of duplicated and reordered payment commands, and 8 end-to-end tests against Kafka and a MongoDB replica set in Testcontainers (happy path, decline, cancel and refund, a late capture after the hold expired, 16 concurrent holds on one seat with exactly one winner, idempotent retries). Each end-to-end test checks the cross-service invariants against both databases. The compose.yaml and curl walkthrough in the README were also run by hand.

### Add behavioural contracts: a CI gate that proves behaviour unchanged

[`914092fb8efd`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/914092fb8efdf4dce60bfcf94c51e6fb159008a8) · [log `9aa1dc1182d6`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/560d5e98-2825-4bc2-90e2-39953d65d9c0/9aa1dc1182d6bd6b849f6eeff1e440ab2c791725270898133b98dbc53b58c7bc.jsonl.gz)

tools/contracts is a dependency-free verifier (Java 25, ClassFile API). For a method it derives a contract, the outcome of every possible input, which is checked in next to the code. The build fails when the bytecode no longer matches it, and an intended change shows up as a reviewable diff of exactly the cases that changed. The contract is a proof, not a sample: purity is proved from bytecode (a closed-world walk through sealed hierarchies, with a short list of trusted JDK APIs), the input domain is derived from enums, booleans, records and sealed types, and every input is executed. Methods that are impure or have unbounded inputs are refused. A Gradle convention plugin adds verifyContracts to check and updateContracts, and writes SARIF for GitHub code scanning and SonarQube. Box Office's OrderLifecycle#decide is the first target: 36 cases.

Why this approach: JBMC 6.11 was tried first and cannot handle modern Java as it ships. It treats the pattern-switch typeSwitch invokedynamic as an unknown value, and has no models for List.of, record equals or Math.multiplyExact; docs/approaches.md records this as B5's finding and the POC as B8. Verified with 7 unit tests of the verifier (pure, static write, clock read, open interface, unbounded domain, diff, update then drift) and by trying three changes on the real code: a case-merging cleanup that kept money for declined orders (caught, 2 cases), a refactor from switch to == that the agent believed equivalent but which changed null handling (caught, 1 case), and an Instant.now() call (refused as impure). A genuinely equivalent refactor passes. ./gradlew build passes with verifyContracts in check.

### Add symbolic, capability and TLA+ verification examples 006 to 012

[`68f6567ca4e3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/68f6567ca4e36d524cf74d031be494b6c75e9973) · [log `5026337d0f66`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/560d5e98-2825-4bc2-90e2-39953d65d9c0/5026337d0f6681bed96ec275fe879101ddcb9e348353838a4481f8ad488bf38b.jsonl.gz)

The first five examples enumerate a finite state machine, which a type system could approximate. This adds three approaches that a type system cannot, each with examples aimed at cloud Java developers: B9 regression verification, B10 capability contracts and D1 protocol model checking. The examples generator (examples/tools/build.py) now has one runner per approach id, the result schema gained verdictLabel, domain, proof, statement, trace and related fields, and the table of contents shows the approach.

B9, regression verification (examples 006 to 008): Equivalence.java in examples/tools/contracts compares two compiled versions of a method with unbounded inputs. It relocates the old classes into a 'before' package by rewriting constant pools (Relocate.java), generates a harness that asserts both versions agree on every input outside an optional --unchanged-unless Java expression, and runs JBMC on the bytecode with java.lang.Math's real class on the classpath. A counterexample is replayed on the JVM; small inputs are searched first so the witness is readable. HoldPolicy.totalCents gained a 10% group discount for six seats or more to have realistic arithmetic to verify. 006 refutes a per-seat rounding refactor, 007 proves a doubled discount confined to seats >= 6 over all 2^96 inputs in 13 s, 008 shows a declared scope (seats >= 8) that a one-formula rewrite violates. Measured limit, recorded in the README: an unchanged region with a 64-bit division on each side does not finish in 10 min with MiniSat, Z3, cvc5 or --refine.

B10, capability contracts (examples 009 and 010): Capabilities.java derives, from a module's compiled classes, every call to a JDK entry point of a capability (clock, console, environment, filesystem, JNDI, native, network, process, randomness, reflection, scripting, serialization, threads) and the libraries called, as src/contract/capabilities.contract, checked by the same verifyContracts task (the Gradle plugin now passes --classes and --module; -Ptarget=capabilities adds the contract). The contracts and ticketing-domain modules have baseline contracts with no capabilities. 009 catches MessageCodec resolving a class named in a Kafka payload with Class.forName, the shape of the Jackson deserialization CVEs; 010 shows a serialization setting that changes nothing.

D1, protocol model checking (examples 011 and 012): examples/apps/boxoffice/spec/BoxOffice.tla models the two services, their outbox relays, Kafka topics, the sweeper and the clock, one action per transaction, with the README's safety invariants. Its order state machine, OrderLifecycleContract.tla, is generated by examples/tools/tla/contract_to_tla.py from the B8 behavioural contract, so the model runs the decisions the bytecode is proven to make. 011 removes the heldBy query in PaymentEventHandler and TLC produces a nine-step trace in which a paid customer's capture event is dead-lettered after the hold expires; 012 deletes the hold sweeper and TLC confirms every invariant in 3,604 states. The generator runs TLC with one worker so the trace is stable.

Verified by running the verifier's 17 unit tests (jbmc installed) and python3 examples/tools/build.py for all twelve examples, each reaching its expected verdict; the first five pages regenerate unchanged apart from the new table column. Documentation updated: examples/README.md (approach table and intro), approaches.md (B9, B10, D1 and the JBMC finding), the contracts README (three contract kinds, limits), the spec README, the Box Office README, the root README and the setup README. These land in one commit because the generator, schemas and tables are shared by all three approaches.

That script installs:

| Formal methods | TLA+ TLC model checker, KeY 3.0.0 (proves JML-annotated Java), Alloy 6.2.0, Dafny (verifies code, then compiles it to Java) |

**Reply:**

I've written the plan for bytecode- and assembly-level verification, replaced the old scripts with a generic Ubuntu/WSL installer, and initialised git in the repo. Nothing is committed yet, and nothing is installed: the installer needs your sudo password, so you have to run it. `setup/ubuntu-wsl/doctor.sh` currently reports every tool as missing, which is expected, and the syntax checks pass.

**Run this in your own terminal:**
```bash
cd ~/code/java-formal-verification
setup/ubuntu-wsl/install.sh      # asks for sudo once, for apt and Docker
exec bash && setup/ubuntu-wsl/doctor.sh
```
Quit Docker Desktop first, since you chose native Docker Engine.

**What the post found that matters here:** Theorem's own OSS Verify pipeline already accepts JVM fuzz targets, though only for "never crashes or hangs" statements. It doesn't say publicly how it turns a JVM program into a RISC-V binary, so that's an open question in the doc.

**Approaches in `docs/approaches.md`, by level:**
- **Bytecode (the main bet):** write a JVM bytecode semantics in Lean with Claude, the way Theorem wrote RISC-V semantics. A Jazzer fuzz test becomes the theorem: "this test passes on every input".
- **Checking that semantics:** run it as an interpreter and compare it against HotSpot and GraalVM on generated class files. This is the post's way of testing that the spec matches reality.
- **Bytecode alternatives:**

- **Log → commits:** the manifest lists jj change IDs, which survive rewrites, and adds git SHAs once commits are pushed. A commit's own git SHA can't appear inside that same commit, so it is filled in on the next sync after a push.

    logs/<sha256>.jsonl.gz         gitignored, published on the CDN

**The summary** has three parts:
- **Header table:** time span, models, token use and a link to the log.
- **Changes:** each commit the session made, with the full message the agent wrote. The commit message is the "what and why" narrative, so the agent has nothing extra to write.
- **Conversation:** each prompt with its final reply, shortened where long. Slash commands and compactions appear as one-line entries.

It is built from the redacted log only, so it is as safe to publish as the log. One summary covers a whole session, because a session is one log. Each commit's tree holds the summary and manifest as they were at that commit, so each committed log has its own matching summary.

**Reply:**

I built Box Office, a concert-ticketing system in `apps/boxoffice/`, and committed it locally. It isn't pushed yet; I'll push when you say so. The build passes with 29 tests, and I also ran the services by hand with Docker Compose and curl.

**The domain.** A customer looks at a concert's seats, holds some for a few minutes, places an order, and pays in the background. A hold either gets all the requested seats or none, and two customers can never hold the same seat.

The interesting case is a slow payment. If the hold expires and someone else takes the seats before the payment comes back, the customer is refunded automatically.

**Capabilities:**

| Capability | Endpoint | Style |
|---|---|---|
| Create a concert | `POST /concerts` | sync |

| Cancel an order (seats go back on sale, refund follows) | `POST /orders/{id}/cancellation` → 202 | async |

### 21. 2026-10-30 19:32 UTC

> Look through the `./docs/approaches.md` file. Let's do a quick and dirty POC with one simple use case implementing one possible approach, which we can then iterate off. Examples of use cases are catching unintentional breaking changes, for example: performance issues, security issues, config issues, or functional issues. Consider the formal verification as a contract -- the only changes in the con
>
> *… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**Reply:**

I built the POC as "behavioural contracts": a build check that proves a method still behaves exactly as its checked-in contract says. It runs in `./gradlew check` and outputs SARIF, which GitHub and SonarQube both import. It's committed locally, not pushed.

**How it works.** For a method, the contract is the complete list of its inputs and the outcome of each one. The tool derives it from the compiled bytecode and stores it as a readable file next to the code, e.g. `decide(DECLINED, PaymentCaptured[seatsStillHeld=true]) => Transition[next=REFUND_PENDING, …]`.
- **Unintended change:** the build fails and lists each input whose outcome changed, with the old and new result.
- **Intended change:** the developer runs `./gradlew updateContracts`, and the pull request diff shows reviewers exactly which cases changed.
- **Refactor that keeps behaviour:** passes without touching the contract.

Nobody writes a spec.

**Why the verdict is a proof, not a test run:**
1. **Purity, checked on the bytecode:** the method can't read the clock, do I/O, write global state, or call code the tool can't see. A short, documented list of JDK methods is trusted as pure.
2. **Finite inputs, derived from the types:** enums, booleans, records and sealed interfaces have finitely many values, so the tool lists them all, null included.
3. **Every input executed:** a pure method with finitely many inputs is fully described by those results.
